beats.script_body: You are about to enter what many call the largest work of art in New York City. Central Park looks like a natural landscape, but almost everything inside it was designed, planted, landscaped, and laid out by human hands. As its designer Frederick Law Olmsted put it, "Every foot of the Park's surface, every tree and bush, as well as every arch, roadway and walk, has been placed where it is with a purpose." It is a nineteenth-century space — a natural environment, a recreational place, a commercial space, and a civic center all at once.

beats.script_body: The park was the work of two men. The American Frederick Law Olmsted, who was not a park designer before Central Park made him one, took charge of the landscaping. The English immigrant Calvert Vaux — pronounced "vawx" — probably the first person to call himself a "landscape architect" rather than a "landscape artist," handled many of the park's structures, helped by architect Jacob Wrey Mould. Olmsted's earlier life was improbable: a small farmer on Staten Island, an agricultural writer, a founder of the Nation magazine, and supervisor of a California gold mine, but best known for his writing on slavery in the South. Vaux had come to America to join landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing, who would have been the most likely candidate to design the park had he not drowned tragically before it began. In 1857, Olmsted landed a job as supervisor of land clearance through influential friends, then teamed up with Vaux to design the winning Greensward Plan. The city's request for proposals had strict requirements, and the pair met them masterfully — a parade ground became the Sheep Meadow, a fire lookout tower became Belvedere Tower, "the castle," a skating area became the Lake, and four cross-streets became the sunken transverse roads hidden below ground level.

beats.source_passage: The two men most responsible for the park's design are the American Frederick Law Olmsted (1822–1903) and the English immigrant Calvert Vaux (1824–1895). Olmsted, who was decidedly not a park designer before Central Park made him one, was responsible for the park's landscaping. Vaux (pronounced "vawx"), who was probably the first person to call himself a "landscape architect" as opposed to a "landscape artist," was responsible for many of the park's structures, helped by architect Jacob Wrey Mould. Olmsted's pre-park experience included being a small farmer on Staten Island, an agricultural writer, a founder of the Nation magazine, and supervisor of a California gold mine. But he was best known for his writing on slavery in the South. Vaux had come to the United States to join a partnership with landscape designer Andrew Jackson Downing, who would have been the most likely candidate for park designer had he not drowned tragically before the project began. Olmsted landed a job in 1857 as the supervisor of land clearance for the park through influential friends. He then teamed up with Vaux to design the winning Greensward Plan for the park. The city's request for proposal had specific design requirements, which Olmsted and Vaux met masterfully. A parade ground became the Sheep Meadow; a fire lookout tower became Belvedere Tower—"the castle"; a skating area became the Lake; and four cross-streets became the four sunken transverse roads that are hidden from view below ground level.

beats.script_body: After Central Park, Olmsted became one of the country's best-known park designers, shaping in whole or in part Prospect and Riverside Parks, Boston's Back Bay Fens, Philadelphia's Fairmont Park, Detroit's Belle Isle, Montreal's Mount Royal, Stanford's campus, and much more. Vaux designed Prospect and Fort Greene Parks with him, plus the Metropolitan Museum, the American Museum of Natural History, and Frederic Church's Olana home, but their partnership ended in 1872. Never as celebrated as Olmsted, Vaux grew bitter in later life. He drowned off the current site of the Brooklyn Navy Yard in 1895, and it is entirely possible he committed suicide.

beats.script_body: The desire for a great city park grew among wealthy New Yorkers in the mid-nineteenth century. Park boosters ranged from writers like William Cullen Bryant and Horace Greeley to real estate speculators like James Beekman and Mayor Fernando Wood. They compared New York unfavorably to European cities with parks, and the wealthy wanted somewhere to ride their carriages away from the hoi polloi of the city streets. There were many competing arguments: that a park would establish New York as the nation's cultural capital, provide a retreat for the rich, and serve as a social safety valve for the poor crammed into tenements with no green space. But the idea of a truly democratic park for all people frightened the middle classes. An 1858 editorial in the New York Herald sneered that when a public park opened, "Sam will air himself in it," knock down any better-dressed man who remonstrated, and turn the park into "nothing but a great beer garden for the lowest denizens of the city." Standing here, you can still ask the questions the park has always provoked: Is a picnic acceptable? Music? Volleyball? Barbecuing? Dancing? What is "respectable," and what is "unacceptable," today?

beats.source_passage: New Yorkers, especially wealthy ones, gradually developed a desire for a city park in the mid–nineteenth century. Park boosters included writers such as William Cullen Bryant and Horace Greeley, real estate speculators such as James Beekman, and Mayor Fernando Wood. They compared New York unfavorably to European cities that had parks. Further, the wealthy wanted a place to ride their carriages away from the hoi polloi of the city streets. There were many competing arguments for the park: for example, that it would establish New York as the nation's cultural capital, provide a retreat for the wealthy, and be a social safety valve for the city's poor, who were crammed into tenement housing with no parks to the south. Interestingly, the desire for a democratic park for all people was frightening to the middle classes and precipitated a debate over the use of public space by "respectable" and "disorderly" classes, as this editorial in the New York Herald of 1858 illustrates: It is folly to expect in this country to have parks like those in old aristocratic countries. When we open a public park, Sam will air himself in it.

beats.script_body: A democratic park did not mean treating those who already lived on the land democratically. Boosters demonized the pre-park inhabitants to make it easier for the city to seize their property. The New York Times, voicing the anti-Irish Catholic bigotry typical of the era, described park residents as "principally Irish families [in] rickety little one storie shanties inhabited by four or five persons, not including the pig and the goats." Other papers played up the "vagabonds" and "scoundrels" supposedly living in the park. Yet more than 90 percent of those living on the future parkland were immigrants — largely Irish and German — or African Americans, and a careful look at the records shows a far higher share of them owned their land than did city dwellers at large. Landowner, renter, and squatter alike were evicted in 1857 and 1858 to make way for construction.

beats.source_passage: Furthermore, a democratic park did not mean treating those who currently lived in what would become parkland democratically. A lot of propaganda and boosterism demonized the pre-park inhabitants of the land to make it easier for the city to take their property. The New York Times, expressing anti–Irish Catholic bigotry typical of the nineteenth century, described park residents as "principally Irish families [in] rickety . . . little one storie shanties . . . inhabited by four or five persons, not including the pig and the goats," and other newspapers made much of the "vagabonds" and "scoundrels" living in the park. More than 90 percent of those living on what would be parkland were either immigrants, largely Irish and German, or African Americans. In the latter case, Seneca Village, whose principal street was in the park across from West Eighty-fifth Street, was a well-established town with a school, three churches, and 250 residents. Indeed, a careful search of records shows that a far higher percentage of people living in the park actually owned their own land than did people in the city at large. Nonetheless, landowner, renter, and squatter alike were evicted in 1857 and 1858 to make way for construction.

beats.script_body: We begin at the giant monument to the Maine, regilded now and shining in the sun. It memorializes the American battleship that blew up — or was blown up — in Havana harbor in 1898, killing over 250 sailors and precipitating the Spanish-American War. William Randolph Hearst, whose New York Journal fervently supported the war, helped raise money for the monument. It was meant to stand in Times Square but never made it there. Look up and you'll see "Columbia Triumphant," the statue at the top, surrounded below by Victory, Peace, Courage, and Fortitude; on the back stand Justice, Warrior, and History; and on the sides the Pacific Ocean as an old man and the Atlantic Ocean as a young man.

beats.script_body: Greyshot Arch is one of over forty bridges Vaux designed with Jacob Wrey Mould. Walk under its sandstone balustrade and through the vaulted, red-brick archway — a passage just over thirty feet wide, ten feet high, and eighty feet long. Continue along the path and take the left fork to reach Pine Bank Arch, two hundred feet beyond. Walk over this cast-iron beauty, whose entire structure was rebuilt with a new wooden floor in 1984. In Central Park, every single arch and every bridge is different.

beats.script_body: Alongside the path rises Umpire Rock, the giant piece of Manhattan schist that supervises the Heckscher Ballfields and the Ballplayers House just to the north. Schist is the bedrock under Manhattan — geologically a combination of mica, quartz, feldspar, and hornblende. Look carefully at the outcroppings here and you'll notice they are smoother on the north side, where glaciers first scraped them, and rougher and more irregular to the south. You can impress friends by telling them that major outcroppings are called roche moutonnée, or "laying sheep," because the glacial cuttings supposedly make them look like sleeping sheep.

beats.script_body: The ball fields seem a perfectly natural part of the park, but recreation had almost nothing to do with the original design. The first park had no playground at all, only three meadows for children's field sports — and to play on them, kids needed a certificate of good attendance and character from their teachers, a hard thing for the many nineteenth-century children who were working rather than in school. Concrete and asphalt playgrounds arrived around the turn of the twentieth century, championed by social reformers who believed playgrounds would save children from gangs and, later, from unemployment. Adult baseball diamonds weren't a serious feature until the 1920s. Olmsted and Vaux had wanted "a ground to which people may easily go after their day's work is done" — a place that completely shut out the city.

beats.script_body: How big is the park, and what did it cost? It runs north-south from 110th Street down to Fifty-ninth Street, and east-west from Fifth Avenue to Central Park West — just over 840 acres, about twice the size of feudal-relic Monaco and several times bigger than Governors Island. In the late 1850s the city paid the landowners of this rocky, swampy farmland almost $7.5 million, only a few hundred thousand dollars more than the United States would soon pay Russia for all of Alaska. Construction began in 1858, and much of the landscaping south of Seventy-ninth Street was finished by December 1860; it took another five years to reach 110th Street, though the park is never truly finished. As far as historians can tell, Irish workers did almost all the labor, there were no black workers, and the only women employed cleaned offices. Crews swelled from about two thousand workers in early spring to thirty-five hundred by late summer. For a ten-hour day, unskilled laborers earning a dollar brought in millions of cubic yards of soil, planted hundreds of non-native trees, laid six and a half miles of road, dug out a 106-acre reservoir, and built mile upon mile of trails.

beats.script_body: The Carousel before you was built in 1908 in Coney Island and moved here in 1951, replacing the park's original 1871 carousel, which burned down. That original was supposedly powered by a blind horse and a blind mule walking a treadmill underneath it. The Carousel runs on a contract from the city. For years Sal Napolitano ran it, until he was outbid by the Makkos Organization — formerly the M & T Pretzel Company — an immigrant success story run by Greek immigrant Themis Makkos and his sons.

beats.script_body: The Sheep Meadow, the large grass field before you, was originally landscaped as a parade ground but began hosting sheep in 1864. Olmsted required a particular breed of Southdown sheep whose gray-and-white coloring offset the grass — he was following William Gilpin, whose book Forest Scenery he loved. Gilpin wrote: "Sheep particularly are very ornamental in a park. Their color is just that dingy hue, which contrasts with the verdure of the ground; and the flakiness of their wool is rich and picturesque." The meadow stayed green until a series of concerts in the 1960s and 1970s killed much of the grass. Replanted in 1979, it stays green today by banning organized sports, concerts, and any activity when the grass is wet.

beats.script_body: A huge inlaid-marble plaque on the ground calls this the Literary Walk, though New Yorkers call it the Mall — the formal promenade at the center of the naturalistic park. A wide, straight pathway bordered by double rows of overhanging elms runs northwest up to Bethesda Terrace. Surprisingly, Olmsted and Vaux did not intend statues anywhere but at Bethesda Terrace; all the rest were forced on them by the city, pressured by civic, ethnic, and religious groups who wanted figures of their great men in the park. At the southern end you'll find Shakespeare from 1870, Sir Walter Scott from 1871, and Robert Burns from 1880.

beats.source_passage: Follow the traffic on the roadway east for less than two hundred feet until you come to the southern end of what a huge, inlaid-marble plaque on the ground asserts is Literary Walk. New Yorkers call it the Mall. The Mall is the formal promenade at the center of the naturalistic park. A wide, straight pathway bordered on both sides by double rows of overhanging elms runs northwest right up to Bethesda Terrace, the formal center of the park. Note the statues at the southern end. Surprisingly, Olmsted and Vaux did not intend statues anywhere but at Bethesda Terrace, which we'll come to shortly. All the rest were forced on them by the city, under pressure from civic, ethnic, and religious groups who wanted figures of their great men in the park. You will see Shakespeare (1870) toward the Mall's eastern entrance, Sir Walter Scott (1871) on your immediate right, and Robert Burns (1880) on your immediate left.

beats.script_body: Further north along the Mall stands the statue of Fitz-Greene Halleck, on your right. Halleck, who died in 1867, was one of the most famous poets in the country in the nineteenth century — though his poems are now almost completely forgotten. That makes it astonishing to learn that when this statue was unveiled in 1876, President Rutherford B. Hayes, his entire cabinet, and ten thousand others came for the ceremony. That no one knows who he is today says volumes about representing people in statues, an idea well past its heyday.

beats.script_body: Can you name the most famous statue of a woman in the park? It's Alice in Wonderland. In fact there are no statues in the park of women who were living, historical figures — all are allegorical figures or characters from nursery rhymes. Across all of Manhattan's public spaces, statues of actual women number only four: Gertrude Stein, Golda Meir, Joan of Arc, and Eleanor Roosevelt.

beats.script_body: Olmsted and Vaux installed a cast-iron bandstand to the west in 1859, but this band shell on your right is a later anachronism: retired banker Elkan Naumburg donated money to build it in 1923. Over the years it has hosted Leonard Bernstein, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman, Martin Luther King Jr., Fidel Castro, and Mayor Fiorello La Guardia selling war bonds during World War II. It was a wildly popular spot for ballroom dancing in the 1940s and 1950s, when the Goldman Band played live. When the city later wanted to tear it down, Naumburg's great-grandson and others sued — and the courts ruled the city had to maintain a gift it had willingly accepted.

beats.source_passage: Olmsted and Vaux installed a cast-iron bandstand to the west in 1859, but the current one is a historical anachronism. In 1923, retired banker Elkan Naumberg donated money to build it. This band shell has hosted Leonard Bernstein, Duke Ellington, Benny Goodman, Martin Luther King Jr, Fidel Castro, and Mayor Fiorello La Guardia selling war bonds during World War II. It was a very popular spot for ballroom dancing in the 1940s and 1950s, when the Goldman Band played here live. But as the popularity of ballroom dancing waned, so did the use of the band shell. The city wanted to tear it down in accordance with plans by the Central Park Conservancy (the nonprofit agency that actually runs the park), but Naumberg's great-grandson and others sued the city. The courts ruled that the city had to maintain it as a gift it had willingly accepted, whether or not it fit with the old-style benches that have been built around it.

beats.script_body: Above the band shell on the hill is Rumsey Playfield, a once-desolate asphalt lot with a storied past, now home to SummerStage and its free concerts. The hill was originally the site of the Ladies Refreshment Pavilion, but in the late 1920s Mayor "Gentleman" Jimmy Walker asked his friend Sidney Solomon to take over the space. Solomon hired Joseph Urban to redesign the interior, which included a black-glass ballroom. Walker and his mistress Betty Compton reviewed the plans personally, and some of the financing even came from Arnold Rothstein — the man who had fixed the 1919 World Series. The building opened as the Central Park Casino, without gambling, in 1929, and became one of the most elegant places to eat in the city until Walker fled office under corruption charges a few years later. In 1934 Robert Moses, then parks commissioner, demolished the casino, arguing that only restaurants "within the reach of persons of average means" belonged in the park. Tellingly, Moses then converted the sheepfold west of the Sheep Meadow into Tavern on the Green — which persons of average means have always found far too expensive.

beats.script_body: On June 22, 1901, the benches along part of the Mall were replaced with new green rocking chairs. The moment a park visitor sat down, a uniformed attendant walked up to demand five cents for a chair with arms, three cents for one without. Entrepreneur Oscar Spate had secured a rocking-chair franchise from Tammany Hall and hoped to make $250 a day here and in other city parks. Instead the angry public rioted, smashing and stealing the chairs. A chastened Parks Commission withdrew Spate's franchise and replaced his chairs with ones marked "For the Exclusive Use of Women and Children, FREE."

beats.script_body: Bethesda Terrace was the only place Olmsted and Vaux wanted any statues, and they ended up with just one. The Moorish building you walked underneath was designed by Jacob Wrey Mould, who had studied Islamic architecture and reproduced its style here; its ceiling was originally covered with thousands of tiles, now being reinstalled by the Central Park Conservancy. Bethesda Fountain is crowned by Emma Stebbins's Angel of the Waters, from 1873 — the only sculpture in the park by a woman. Stebbins was the sister of the president of the Central Park Board of Commissioners. The fountain refers to the pool in Jerusalem named in the Gospel of John: "There is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda." In the Bible, the sick waited at the pool for an angel to stir the waters, then entered to be cured. There's even a long-running debate over whether Stebbins's angel is a man or a woman — some see a proto-feminist celebration of women, while others note that angels are sexless and the statue simply reflects the design conventions of its day.

beats.script_body: Bow Bridge is one of seven cast-iron bridges built in the park. Seen from ground level on the side, it really is shaped roughly like a bow. Stand on it and look west along Central Park West, and you'll see the low-peaked, verdigrised roofs of the Dakota with a flagpole on top — perhaps Manhattan's most famous apartment building. When it was built in the mid-1880s there was very little this far north; today most people know it as the building where John Lennon lived, and where he was shot. To the left and right of the Dakota stand two of Central Park West's twin-towered apartment buildings, the Majestic and the San Remo.

beats.script_body: No account of Central Park is complete without crime. For whatever reason, crimes in the park carry national resonance while crimes elsewhere in the city usually don't — likely because so many Americans imagine the park as a sanctuary, so that violence here feels like an assault on the body politic. Early arrests were mostly for driving carriages too fast. The first robbery-murder, in 1872, moved the New York Times to remark, "Murder has actually stained the turf of that green fairy land." In the 1880s the Police Gazette warned of "murderous attacks upon the chastity of pure-minded young females" — meaning flashers. Homeless men, "tramps" in the vernacular, drew the papers' ire too; the New York Tribune wrote in the 1870s that "tramps and other unpleasant people [have] quit their winter quarters for the benches in the Park," and that ladies and children hesitated to venture into the Ramble without escorts. Today the park has its own police precinct with the lowest violent-crime rate of any in the city, though the occasional horrific assault still draws enormous attention.

beats.script_body: Vaux designed the castle to serve as a fire watchtower. It sits atop 135-foot-high Vista Rock, through which — beneath your feet — a tunnel is blasted for the Seventy-ninth Street transverse road. If the castle is open, climb the stairs to one of the lookouts. The original castle had no glass in its windows; the structure was meant to deteriorate as the park grew around it, showing people that the work of human hands is ephemeral while nature is eternal. Since 1920, the official weather-reading station for New York City has stood atop the castle and in the fenced-in area behind it, where instruments measure wind, sunshine, temperature, precipitation, and humidity.

beats.script_body: From the castle, look north over the redone Turtle Pond to the 1960 Delacorte Theater, home of free Shakespeare in the Park, and beyond to the giant green ball fields of the Great Lawn. The lawn sits on the site of an 1840s reservoir that was drained in 1930. Until the early 1990s it hosted the park's giant free concerts and gatherings — Elton John in 1980, Simon and Garfunkel in 1981, an antinuclear rally in 1982, Diana Ross in 1983, Paul Simon in 1991, and a Billy Graham gathering the same year, each drawing hundreds of thousands. The Central Park Conservancy then spent over $18 million renovating it with irrigation, drainage, soil, Kentucky bluegrass, and perennial rye. No more large events will take place on it.

beats.script_body: The largest town on the land that became Central Park was Seneca Village, which stretched from Seventy-ninth to Eighty-sixth Streets west of today's Great Lawn, its main street running east-west into the parkland at what is now Eighty-fifth Street. In 1855, two years before its residents were evicted, the village had 264 residents — about three-quarters black, the rest Irish — with homes, gardens, three churches, cemeteries, a school, and a spring that still bubbles up east of Eighty-second Street. It began in 1825, when John and Elizabeth Whitehead started selling parts of their farm to black New Yorkers. The first buyer was Andrew Williams, a twenty-five-year-old bootblack, who bought three lots for $125. Members of the African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church, "Mother Zion," followed, and by 1829 there were nine houses. When the old Croton reservoir displaced the black community of York Hill, many moved here too. Contrary to the accounts that demonized park residents as squatters, Seneca Village's tax and housing records show several two- and three-story buildings, one even with a wraparound porch on three sides.

beats.source_passage: The largest town in the land that would become Central Park was Seneca Village (the origins of the name are still being debated), which stretched from Seventy-ninth to Eighty-sixth Streets to the west of the Great Lawn. Its main street ran east-west into the parkland at what is today Eighty-fifth Street. In 1855, two years before all its residents were evicted, Seneca Village had 264 residents (about three-quarters black and the rest Irish), homes, gardens, three churches, cemeteries, a school, and a spring that still bubbles up in the park east of Eighty-second Street. All that is left today are the cornerstones of one of the churches. How Seneca Village came to be is one of the most interesting stories in the park. Beginning in 1825, John and Elizabeth Whitehead started selling parts of their farm to black New Yorkers. The first buyer was Andrew Williams, a twenty-five-year-old bootblack, who bought three lots for $125. Williams was followed by members of the African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Zion Church, "Mother Zion," from downtown. By 1829 there were nine houses on the side. The building of the now-demolished old reservoir (not the new one that's still there), which was part of the Croton Aqueduct system at the center of the park from 1825 to 1832 displaced another black community known as York Hill, and many of its residents moved to Seneca Village. Contrary to mid-nineteenth-century accounts that demonized residents of the park as "vagabonds" or "squatters," the tax and housing records of Seneca Village tell a different story. Assessors' maps show several twoand three-story buildings, one even with a wraparound porch on three sides.

beats.script_body: For black New Yorkers, land in Seneca Village meant more than homes and income — it meant the vote. In 1821, New York revised its constitution to grant universal white male suffrage but required free blacks to own $250 worth of property to vote. By 1855 there were twelve thousand black residents in New York but only one hundred black voters — and ten of them lived in Seneca Village. Black residents there were far more likely to own property than whites elsewhere in the city. About three-quarters of the villagers regularly attended one of its three churches, among them All Angels' Church, built in 1849 by the white Reverend Thomas Peters for a black and German congregation.

beats.script_body: Seneca Village's All Angels' Church housed Colored School No. 3, whose black teacher struck a blow for equality a full century before Rosa Parks. In July 1854, the teacher, twenty-four-year-old Elizabeth Jennings, boarded a Third Avenue streetcar downtown on her way to church. The car carried no sign reading "Colored People Allowed in This Car," as others did, and when Jennings refused to get off, she was forcibly removed by the conductor and a policeman. She sued the Third Avenue Railway Company and was represented at her 1855 trial by another twenty-four-year-old: the future president Chester A. Arthur. The jury ruled that under state law the railway was a common carrier "bound to carry all respectable people," and that colored persons, if sober, well-behaved, and free from disease, had the same rights as others. The third Seneca Village church, AME Zion — the oldest black church in New York, founded in 1796 — counted among its members Sojourner Truth, Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, and Thomas Fortune.

beats.script_body: Not even the churches could save the community when the park came. A city commission surveyed and assessed every lot, and those inside the future park were taken by eminent domain — the government forcibly, but with pay, taking land for what it declares the common good. The city paid Andrew Williams, the first property owner, $2,335 for his two-story house and three lots; Williams argued in vain that the house alone was worth $1,400 and that he'd been offered $3,500 for house and lots. The New-York Daily Times introduced white readers to the village in jarring terms, calling it a "neat little settlement, known as 'nigger village,'" whose inhabitants made "a pleasing contrast" to the Irish elsewhere in the park's domain. By 1857 Seneca Village was gone, its residents scattered, its history unknown to most who walk the park today.

beats.source_passage: Alas, not even churches were enough to preserve the community when it came time to build the park. A city commission surveyed and assessed the value of all lots in and around the park. Those inside the park's future limits were taken from their owners by right of eminent domain, which means the government forcibly, but with pay, takes your land for what it declares is the common good. The city paid Andrew Williams, the first property owner, $2,335 for his two-story house and three lots. Williams argued to no avail that the value of the house alone was $1,400 and that he had been offered $3,500 for house and lots. About this time, the New-York Daily Times introduced white New Yorkers to black residents of Seneca Village as a contrast to Irish residents elsewhere in the park's domain: "West of the reservoir within the limits of the Central Park, lies a neat little settlement, known as "nigger village." The Ebon inhabitants after whom the village is called, present a pleasing contrast in their habits and the appearance of their dwellings to the Celtic occupants. How gently they went is unknown, but almost every property owner protested vehemently that the city was not paying fair market value for their land. Nonetheless, by 1857, Seneca Village was gone. Its residents scattered among many neighborhoods, and their history is unknown to most who walk through the park today.

beats.script_body: Near Turtle Pond stands the statue of King Jagiello on horseback, by Stanislaw Ostrowski. It was meant for Kraków, but instead appeared at the Polish pavilion at the 1939–40 World's Fair, and the Polish government in exile gave it to New York in 1945. Jagiello was actually a grand duke of Lithuania who married the Polish queen to unite the two lands.

beats.script_body: This two-hundred-ton obelisk, also known as Cleopatra's Needle, was erected in the park in 1881, but it was first installed in Egypt in the fourteenth century B.C. by Thutmosis III. Over the next twenty-five hundred years it was vandalized by those who carved on, burned, and eventually buried it. The United States was offered the needle in the nineteenth century, and it sailed from Egypt to New York in 1880, with William Vanderbilt paying the hundred-thousand-dollar shipping cost. It landed at West Ninety-sixth Street and was rolled along on cannonballs and giant timbers to railroad tracks, then inched forward as workers picked up the track behind it and laid it in front, over and over — work that took 112 days to reach this spot. On January 22, 1881, the obelisk was pivoted upright into place in under five minutes. Contrary to what's often written, New York pollution has barely altered its surface: most of the blackening is fire damage from the Persians' sacking of Heliopolis thousands of years ago, and its long burial caused salt to crystallize within, making it vulnerable to freezing and thawing.

beats.script_body: East Drive was built for elegant carriages, not cars. There was a New York tradition of a formal carriage procession that entered the park at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South, rolled up East Drive, and crossed Bethesda Terrace to the west side. Commercial wagons were banned when the park opened, and for years police refused entry to anyone not driving a "pleasure carriage." Then in 1899 Winslow E. Buzby drove in the first auto, testing the commissioner's ban with what he called an "automobile victoria-phaeton." Given a summons, Buzby went before a magistrate, who ruled that under the ordinance allowing "pleasure carriages, bicycles, or horseback" his car counted as a pleasure carriage. The park board changed the rules to ban "horseless carriages and motor wagons," but soon relented — and the drives were asphalted beginning in 1912.

beats.source_passage: As you pass under East Drive, remember that it was built for elegant carriages, not cars. In fact, there was a New York City tradition of a formal carriage procession that entered the park at Fifth Avenue and Central Park South and proceeded up East Drive and then across Bethesda Terrace to the west side. Commercial wagons were banned from the park when it opened, and police would refuse entry to anyone not driving a "pleasure carriage" onto the drive for many years after the park opened. Alas, the first auto was driven into the park in 1899 by Winslow E. Buzby, who tested the park commissioner's ban with what he called an "automobile victoria-phaeton." Buzby was given a summons and appeared before a magistrate, who ruled that under the city ordinance that said, "The drive shall be used only by persons in pleasure carriages, on bicycles, or on horseback," Buzby's car was a pleasure carriage. In response, the park board changed the rules to ban "horseless carriages and motor wagons" but soon relented. Nonetheless, change was relentless, and the park's drives were asphalted beginning in 1912.

beats.script_body: The Metropolitan Museum is today one of the largest art museums in the world, with almost three and a half million items ranging from prehistory to a few decades ago. In 1872, Olmsted and Vaux reluctantly allowed a museum on this spot, since the view to it was then blocked by the walls of the reservoir on the Great Lawn. The museum was built in many pieces: the first building, designed by Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould in 1871 and opened in 1880, is almost completely hidden inside the many later additions. The Met stayed closed on Sundays until 1891, when it was forced open by protests from workers who wanted to visit on their only day off and by the city, which threatened to withhold funds.
